title: Graceful degradation: serve less instead of failing
summary: Decide in advance what to drop when things break: kill switches, priority load shedding, stale caches, static fallbacks, deadline budgets and cells that limit blast radius.
principle: Rank every feature and every request by how much it matters, and design a cheaper path for everything below the top. When a dependency fails or load exceeds capacity, turn off or simplify the low-value parts first so the core journey keeps working for as many users as possible. Decide these trade-offs before the incident, not during it.
why:
Most outages are partial: one dependency is slow, one region is overloaded, one shard is hot. A system built as all-or-nothing turns any partial failure into a total one, because the page waits on its slowest call or every request queues behind work that does not matter.

Degradation turns that into a dial. A product page without recommendations is still a product page; checkout with yesterday's delivery estimate still takes money; a search that returns cached results is better than a 503. The tools are simple but need preparation: **feature flags and kill switches** you can flip in seconds, **load shedding** that rejects low-priority work first, **stale caches** and **static fallbacks**, a **deadline budget** that stops waiting when an answer is no longer useful, and **cells** so a failure stays small.

diagrams.title: A product page with a fallback for every optional part
diagrams.alt: Architecture diagram. A product page service calls pricing, which is critical, and reviews and recommendations, which are optional. Reviews fall back to a stale cached copy and recommendations fall back to a static best-sellers list. Pricing has no fallback, so the page fails only if pricing fails.
diagrams.caption: Only one box on this page is allowed to fail the request. Everything else has a cheaper answer ready.

steps.text: The page has an overall deadline of 800 ms. Everything it does must fit inside it, so calls run in parallel with their own shorter timeouts.
Pricing is **critical**: showing a wrong or missing price is worse than an error. If pricing fails, the page fails, and that is a deliberate choice.
Reviews are slow today. After 250 ms the page stops waiting and serves the last cached copy, even if it is a day old. Stale beats empty.
An operator has flipped the recommendations kill switch, so the page does not call it at all and shows a static best-sellers list instead. No timeout is spent.

diagrams.title: Priority load shedding at the edge
diagrams.alt: Sequence diagram. Under overload, the gateway checks the priority of each request. A checkout request is admitted and served. A background prefetch request is rejected immediately with 503 and a Retry-After header. When the backlog is still high, even browse traffic gets a cached, simplified response.
diagrams.caption: Rejecting cheap, low-value work early keeps capacity for the requests that make money. A fast 503 is cheaper than a slow timeout.

messages.label: admit? load 130%
messages.note: Admission control compares in-flight work or queue delay to capacity, not just CPU.

messages.label: GET /prefetch (low)
messages.note: Background prefetch is the lowest tier. Nobody is waiting for it.

messages.label: 503 + Retry-After: 30
messages.note: Rejected in microseconds, before any work. The client backs off and retries later.

messages.label: 200 cached home page
messages.note: Normal-tier traffic is served from a cached, simplified version until load drops. A brownout, not a blackout.

diagrams.title: One shared fleet versus isolated cells
diagrams.alt: Side-by-side comparison. With one shared fleet, a single bad tenant or bad deploy overloads the shared database and every customer is affected. With cells, customers are split across independent copies of the stack behind a thin router, so the same failure only affects the customers in one cell.
diagrams.caption: Cells do not make failures rarer; they make each one smaller. A bad deploy rolled out cell by cell also stops at the first cell.

diagrams.title: Spending an 800 ms deadline budget
diagrams.alt: Bar chart of an illustrative 800 millisecond request budget. Gateway and auth take 60 ms, pricing 300 ms, reviews are capped at 250 ms, rendering takes 90 ms, leaving a reserve of 100 ms.
diagrams.caption: Illustrative numbers. Each hop gets a slice and passes the remaining deadline downstream, so nobody keeps working on an answer the user has already given up on.

diagrams.title: A brownout instead of an outage
diagrams.alt: Timeline of an illustrative incident. A recommendations database slows down and page latency climbs. An alert fires, the on-call flips the recommendations kill switch and latency recovers within a minute. The database is fixed later and recommendations are re-enabled gradually.
diagrams.caption: Because the kill switch existed and was tested, the user-facing impact lasted minutes and the real fix could happen calmly.

events.label: The recommendations database starts a slow full-table scan after a bad query change.
Product page p99 rises from 400 ms to 3 s; page threads wait on recommendations.
Page latency SLO burn-rate alert fires.
On-call flips the recommendations kill switch; pages show a static best-sellers list.
p99 back under 500 ms. Shoppers see a simpler page, not an error.

diagrams.title: Degradation tools by effort and experience kept
diagrams.alt: Trade-off chart with user experience kept on the vertical axis and effort to build on the horizontal axis. Failing hard keeps nothing. A static fallback is cheap and keeps a little. Kill switches and serving stale cache are moderate effort and keep a lot. Priority load shedding takes more work. Cell architecture is the most effort and limits the blast radius the most.
diagrams.caption: Positions are a rough guide. Kill switches and stale caches are the cheapest big wins; cells are a platform investment.

examples.title: Optional data with a deadline and a fallback

bad.label: Await everything; any failure fails the page

good.label: Critical call can fail; optional calls degrade
good.code:
const deadline = Date.now() + 800
const optional = <T>(p: Promise<T>, ms: number, fallback: () => T) =>
  withTimeout(p, Math.min(ms, deadline - Date.now())).catch(() => fallback())

const [price, reviews, recs] = await Promise.all([
  pricing.get(sku, { deadline }),                          // critical: may throw
  optional(reviewsApi.get(sku), 250, () => reviewCache.get(sku) ?? null),
  flags.on('recs') ? optional(recsApi.get(user, sku), 200, () => BEST_SELLERS) : BEST_SELLERS,
])
return render({ price, reviews, recs, degraded: !reviews || recs === BEST_SELLERS })

examples.why: Each optional call has a timeout inside the overall deadline and a cheaper answer when it fails. The kill switch skips recommendations entirely without a deploy. The `degraded` flag lets the page and the metrics show that a fallback was used.

examples.title: Shed by priority, early and cheaply

bad.label: Queue everything until the server falls over

good.label: Reject low tiers first when in-flight work is high

examples.why: An unbounded queue makes every request slow, including the important ones, and the work done for requests that already timed out is wasted. Rejecting by tier keeps the critical path fast; `Retry-After` tells well-behaved clients when to come back.

checklist: Every feature on a critical page is labelled critical or optional, and optional ones have a written fallback.
Kill switches exist for expensive or risky features, can be flipped in seconds without a deploy, and are exercised regularly.
Requests carry a deadline; each hop uses the remaining budget and stops work once it has passed.
Load shedding rejects by priority before doing work, returns 503 with `Retry-After`, and is metered per tier.
Caches can serve stale data when the source is down, with a maximum staleness you have agreed on.
A static fallback (default content, cached page) exists for the most important read paths.
Blast radius is bounded: cells or shards, and deploys rolled out cell by cell.
Degraded responses are visible in metrics and, where it matters, to the user.

antipatterns.title: Fallbacks that were never tested

bad.label: A kill switch nobody has flipped in a year
bad.code:
flags:
  recommendations:
    enabled: true   # 'off' path last run: never

better.label: Exercise the degraded path on purpose
better.code:
game_day:
  monthly:
    - flip: recommendations=off   # in one cell, 10 minutes
      expect: page_p99 < 500ms and error_rate unchanged

antipatterns.why: A fallback that has never run is a guess. It may throw, call the same broken dependency, or overload something else. Regular drills prove it works and keep operators confident to use it.

antipatterns.title: The fallback depends on what failed

bad.label: Fallback reads from the same database
bad.code:
catch { return db.query('SELECT * FROM recs_backup WHERE sku = $1', [sku]) }
// same overloaded database as the primary path

better.label: Fallback from an independent, cheap source

antipatterns.why: When the database is the problem, sending fallback traffic to it adds load at the worst moment. Fallbacks should be cheaper and independent: in-process caches, CDN copies or bundled defaults.

antipatterns.title: Retrying instead of shedding

bad.label: Overloaded server answers slowly; clients retry
bad.code:
server at 130% -> responses take 10 s -> clients time out
-> clients retry -> server at 200%

better.label: Shed fast and tell clients when to return
better.code:
server at 130% -> low tier gets 503 + Retry-After in 1 ms
-> clients back off with jitter -> load falls to 100%

antipatterns.why: Slow answers under overload trigger timeouts and retries, which add even more load. Fast, explicit rejection of low-value work breaks the loop.

interview: When drawing a page or API that fans out, label each dependency critical or optional and say what each optional one falls back to.
Say the magic words with specifics: "Recommendations sit behind a kill switch and fall back to a static list; reviews serve stale cache up to a day old."
Explain load shedding by priority: checkout is never shed before prefetch, and rejection happens before work with 503 and Retry-After.
Mention deadline propagation: a 1 s client timeout means downstream work after 1 s is wasted, so pass the remaining budget along.
At SSE level, talk about blast radius: cells, shuffle sharding or per-tenant limits, and rolling deploys cell by cell, plus game days to test fallbacks.

quiz.question: Under overload, which request should be shed first?
quiz.explain: Shed the work with the least value and nobody waiting for it. Prefetch can be retried later at no cost to the user; checkout and login are the core journey.

quiz.question: Why reject with a fast 503 instead of queueing requests during overload?
choices: Queued requests get slow, time out on the client, and the work is wasted
quiz.explain: Long queues make every request slow, including the important ones, and clients that have given up trigger retries. A fast rejection keeps latency low for admitted work.

quiz.question: Reviews are down. Which fallback is usually best for a product page?
choices: Serve the last cached reviews, even if a day old
quiz.explain: Reviews are optional and change slowly, so slightly stale data is far better than an error or a long wait. Retrying adds load to a failing service.

quiz.question: What do cells mainly improve?
choices: The blast radius of a failure or a bad deploy
quiz.explain: Cells split customers across independent copies of the stack. A failure in one cell affects only its share of customers, and deploys can stop after the first cell.

quiz.question: Why should a fallback not call the same database as the primary path?
choices: If that database is the problem, the fallback adds load to it and fails too
It would return the wrong data
quiz.explain: Fallbacks run exactly when something is struggling. They must be cheaper and independent: local caches, CDN copies or bundled defaults.

practice.prompt: Black Friday is coming. Your e-commerce site has a home page, search, product pages with reviews and recommendations, cart and checkout. Traffic may reach three times capacity. How do you make the site degrade gracefully?
practice.answer: First rank features: checkout, cart and pricing are critical; search and product pages are important; reviews, recommendations, personalised home and prefetch are optional. Put every optional feature behind a kill switch that works without a deploy, and test each one in a game day before the event. Give pages an overall deadline (for example 800 ms) and give each optional call a short timeout with a fallback: stale cached reviews, a static best-sellers list, a cached non-personalised home page from the CDN. Add priority load shedding at the gateway: when in-flight work passes a threshold, reject low tiers first with 503 and Retry-After, and never shed checkout before browsing. Serve search from cache for popular queries if the index is overloaded. Split traffic into cells so a failure or bad deploy hits only part of the customers, and freeze deploys or roll them cell by cell. Watch SLO dashboards per tier and a 'degraded responses' metric so operators know which switches are on.
rubric: Ranks features into critical and optional before choosing mechanisms
Kill switches that need no deploy, tested in advance
Timeouts within a deadline budget, with independent fallbacks (stale cache, static content)
Priority load shedding with 503 and Retry-After, protecting checkout
Limits blast radius with cells or shards and careful deploys
